title: A.2 Forces and Momentum
subject: IBDP Physics
introduction: Forces describe interactions between objects and explain why motion changes. In physics, forces are responsible for acceleration, changes in direction and changes in the energy of systems. Understanding forces and momentum allows scientists and engineers to predict how objects move and interact.

definitions.meaning: A push or pull that changes the motion or shape of an object. Force is a vector quantity measured in newtons (N).
The amount of matter in an object. Mass is measured in kilograms (kg).
The gravitational force acting on an object due to a gravitational field.
The quantity of motion possessed by an object. Momentum depends on mass and velocity.
The change in momentum caused by a force acting over a time interval.
The tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion.

core_concepts.heading: Newton's First Law
core_concepts.explanation: An object remains at rest or continues moving with constant velocity unless acted upon by an external resultant force. This property is called inertia.

core_concepts.heading: Newton's Second Law
core_concepts.explanation: The acceleration of an object depends on the resultant force acting on it and its mass. Greater force produces greater acceleration, while greater mass reduces acceleration.

core_concepts.heading: Newton's Third Law
core_concepts.explanation: When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other. These forces act on different objects.

core_concepts.heading: Resultant Force
core_concepts.explanation: The resultant force is the overall force acting on an object after considering all individual forces and their directions.

force_types.name: Gravitational Force
force_types.explanation: Gravitational force is the attractive force between objects with mass. Near the surface of Earth, this force is called weight.

force_types.name: Normal Reaction Force
force_types.explanation: The normal reaction force is the support force exerted by a surface on an object. It acts perpendicular to the surface.

force_types.name: Friction
force_types.explanation: Friction opposes the relative motion between surfaces. It depends on the type of surfaces and the normal force.

force_types.name: Tension
force_types.explanation: Tension is the pulling force transmitted through strings, ropes or cables when they are stretched.

force_types.name: Drag Force
force_types.explanation: Drag is a resistive force caused by movement through a fluid such as air or water.

free_body_diagrams.explanation: A free body diagram represents all external forces acting on an object. It helps analyse the resultant force and predict acceleration.
steps: Draw the object as a simple shape.
Identify all forces acting on the object.

formulas.name: Newton's Second Law
formulas.explanation: The resultant force acting on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration.

formulas.name: Weight
formulas.explanation: Weight depends on the mass of an object and the gravitational field strength.

formulas.name: Momentum
formulas.explanation: Momentum describes the quantity of motion of an object.

formulas.name: Impulse
formulas.explanation: Impulse describes how a force changes the momentum of an object.

worked_examples.question: A 5 kg object accelerates at 4 m/s². Calculate the resultant force.
A 2 kg ball moves at 8 m/s. Calculate its momentum.

momentum_and_collisions.explanation: Momentum is conserved in an isolated system where no external resultant force acts. The total momentum before an interaction is equal to the total momentum after the interaction.
momentum_and_collisions.formula: total momentum before = total momentum after
momentum_and_collisions.importance: This principle is used to analyse collisions and explosions.

momentum_and_collisions.explanation: An elastic collision is an interaction where both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. Objects separate after collision without permanent deformation.
An inelastic collision conserves momentum but not kinetic energy. Some kinetic energy changes into heat, sound or deformation energy.
During an explosion, objects move apart because internal forces convert stored energy into kinetic energy. Total momentum remains conserved if external forces are ignored.

applications: Vehicle airbags increase collision time, reducing the force experienced by passengers.
Rocket propulsion uses conservation of momentum to produce thrust.
Sports equipment is designed using principles of force and momentum.
Engineers use force analysis to design bridges, aircraft and machines.
common_mistakes: Using mass instead of weight when calculating forces.
Forgetting that force is a vector quantity and has direction.
Adding forces without considering their directions.
Forgetting that momentum is conserved only when external forces are negligible.
Assuming Newton's third law forces act on the same object.
ib_exam_tips: Always draw a free body diagram before solving force questions.
Identify the system before applying conservation of momentum.
Use arrows to show directions of forces and velocities.
State the principle used in calculations.
Include units in every final answer.
Explain Newton's laws using correct physics vocabulary.

hl_extension.explanation: In circular motion, a resultant force directed towards the centre of the circle provides centripetal acceleration.
When drag force becomes equal to weight, the resultant force becomes zero and an object continues falling at constant velocity.
Higher level physics analyses momentum conservation using vector components in different directions.

practice_questions.question: A force of 15 N acts on a 3 kg object. Calculate acceleration.
A 4 kg object moving at 6 m/s collides with another object. Calculate its initial momentum.
Explain why airbags reduce injuries during collisions.
practice_questions.answer: Airbags increase the time taken for momentum change, reducing the force according to impulse.

summary: Forces and momentum explain how objects interact and change their motion. Newton's laws provide the foundation for analysing forces, while momentum conservation allows prediction of outcomes in collisions and explosions. These principles are essential in mechanics and many engineering applications.
